senses.gloss:
Sikhism
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Whether सिखिस्म् is a part of हिन्दुइस्म् as enunciated in the Constitution of India (Article 25.2B; explanation 11) or a separate and independent religion, depends on the way one looks at it.
If its acceptance of the theory of कर्म and rebirth, सṁसार (transmigratory existence) and मुक्ति (liberation) through ज्ञान (knowledge) and भक्ति (devotion to God and faith in his grace) are the criterion then it becomes a part of हिन्दुइस्म्.
If its rejection of the Vedic religion of sacrifices and rituals, the vehement criticism of the चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् and denunciation of इमगे wओर्स्हिप् are given prominence, it can be considered as being outside the pale of orthodox हिन्दुइस्म्.
It may be safer to assume that it is a vigorous reform movement against the degenerated forms of हिन्दुइस्म् that existed during its origin and growth.
The Gurus
Guru Nānak (A. D. 1469-1539) was the founder of सिखिस्म् (See NĀNAK, GURU for details.) He was followed by a succession of nine more Gurus, the pontifical tradition ending with गुरु Gobind Singh (A. D. 1666-1708), the tenth in the series.
Though each one of them contributed to the growth and success of the Sikh movement, that of the last गुरु was, by any standard, significant. It was गुरु Gobind Singh who transformed सिखिस्म् into a dynamic religion and the Sikhs into a race of warriors in defence of their धर्म.
Again, it was he who terminated the गुरु-tradition with himself as the last गुरु and declared that the Granth Sāhib would hereafter fill that place with all the respect due to the गुरु and has to be venerated as such.
Guru Granth Sāhib
The Guru Granth Sāhib is the Scripture of the Sikhs even as the वेदस् are for the Hindus, the Bible for the Christians and the Qurān for the Muslims. (See GRANTH SĀHIB for details.)
It was compiled by गुरु Arjan Dev (A. D. 1563-1606) in A. D. 1604 with the help of Bhai Gurudas.
It is also called Ādi Granth (the Original or the Primary Book).
The Daśam Granth is the secondary scripture containing the writings of the tenth गुरु, Gobind Singh. Some of its hymns are used in Sikh worship.
Metaphysics
Sikhism accepts only one God. He can have two aspects: without attributes (Nirguṇa) and with attributes (Saguṇa). The former is called Ek-Oṅkār and the latter, Oṅkār.
In reality these two aspects are one and the same.
God endowed with his power of māyā is the creator of this universe. In this aspect, he is also called Parabrahma and ईश्वर. He is dayālu (kind) and kṛpālu (benevolent). Thus he becomes an object of worship and devotion.
Māyā has the peculiar power of concealing God and give rise to five evils which bind the human beings. They are: काम (lust), krodha (anger), लोभ (greed), मोह (infatuation) and अहङ्कार (egoism, pride).
Human beings can free themselves from these five evils only by the grace of God.
According to सिखिस्म् God does not incarnate himself in this world.
Other names used for God are: Satnāma (Holy name), Kartār (Creator), Akāl (Eternal), Allāh, Khudā and Paravardigār (Cherisher). In later literature, Wahe-गुरु is also used as his name.
Man is an embodied सोउल्. The सोउल् is immortal but the body is not. Man as the सोउल् is like a spark from a blazing fire or like the water of the ocean kept in a tumbler. Body is the greatest bondage. To get मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् he has to put an end to transmigration. Bondage has been caused by the five evils stated above. When the divinity in him makes him gurumukh (turn towards God) and prevents him from becoming manmukh (turn towards the evils of the मिन्द्) and he surrenders to the will of God, he is freed by His grace.
This world is a wonderful च्रेअतिओन् of God, his līlā or sport. It is real but dependent on him. Hence everyone has to perform his duty properly, please God by it and win his release by His grace.
Man can realise God only with the help of a sadguru. To realise the Nirguṇa aspect he has to follow the path of ज्ञान consisting of three steps: suniyai (= śravaṇa) (listening to the गुरु); mannai (= मनन) (pondering over it); and ध्यान (= निदिध्यासन) (deep meditation).
To realise the Saguṇa aspect or ईश्वर, the path of devotion has to be adopted. Here nāmasumirana (= nāma-smaraṇa) or constant utterance of God’s name as also total surrender to him are the disciplines recommended. Release comes by the grace of God which is his gift.
The released सोउल् attains Sac-khaṇḍ, the eternal abode of God and lives there happily.
The unreleased सोउल् has to undergo countless rebirths according to his कर्म.
Epilogue
It is thus seen that सिखिस्म् and हिन्दुइस्म् have many things in common. It is also a historical fact that the Sikhs have often fought for—and even sacrificed their lives in defence of—Hinduism. Conse-quently, the social relationship between the Sikhs and the Hindus is quite close and intimate.

Śikhaṇḍin
------------------------------------------
Ambā, the eldest daughter of the king of काशी, was forcibly taken away from the court during her स्वयṁवर (marriage by choice) by भीष्म, along with her two sisters अम्बिका and Ambālikā. Since neither the king Saubha whom she had loved nor भीष्म who abducted her agreed to marry her, she vowed to kill भीष्म in her next birth. (See AMBĀ for details.)
She was reborn as the daughter of the king Drupada but was brought up as a son. Later, due to the grace of a यक्ष, Sthūṇākarṇa by name, she became a man and was named शिखण्डिन्.
Prince शिखण्डिन् trained by Droṇā-cārya, became a great warrior. He married the daughter of the king Hiraṇyavarma of the country Daśārṇa and had two sons from her.
He fought the Kauravas on behalf of the Pāṇḍavas. Since भीष्म, who knew the whole truth, refused to fight with him, अर्जुन kept him in front of himself and shot भीष्म, who now retired from the battlefield.
Śikhaṇḍin was killed by Aśvatthāma in sleep along with the other warriors of the Pāṇḍava army, towards the end of the कुरुक्षेत्र war.
See also BHĪṢMA.

śikhara
(‘that which has a top’)
------------------------------------------
The words गोपुर, शिखर and विमान are generally assumed to be synonymous, but are not.
Gopura is the huge tower built over the entrance of big temples. विमान is a small tower built over the गर्भगृह (sanctum sanctorum) to indicate the place where the chief deity is installed. शिखर is the uppermost tapering part of the विमान. Over the शिखर is built the आमलक (myroballan-shaped structure) capped by a कलश (finial).
See also GOPURA.
